note.question: Does removing drivers' right to reject e-hail requests improve matching efficiency, earnings, and rider welfare enough to compensate for the loss of agent autonomy?
note.overview: The article estimates a finite-horizon dynamic game in which many strategic taxi drivers choose e-hail acceptance and relocation while riders respond to fares and expected waits. Driver beliefs and rider demand are joined in a mean-field competitive two-sided-market equilibrium.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: At each five-minute period, riders choose a transport mode; the platform broadcasts e-hail requests; drivers decide whether to enter each e-hail matching pool; unmatched drivers search for street-hail riders; matched drivers travel and unmatched drivers choose where to relocate. This repeats over a finite day shift, and beliefs, wait times, demand, and spatial supply must be mutually consistent. Acceptance and relocation by many drivers determine the spatial supply state, which determines rider wait times and demand. The driver-accept regime preserves private trip selection; the auto-accept regime centralizes assignment and removes screening frictions.
